common_name: Alphonse Karr Bamboo (Golden Striped Hedge Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this is a true clumping bamboo with tight rhizomes and needs no barrier, unlike the running Phyllostachys types.

directions: Alphonse Karr is a sun-loving hedge bamboo selection with slender golden-yellow culms marked by irregular green stripes running the length of the cane, and new shoots often flush pink to red where exposed to strong sunlight, an effect that fades as the culm matures. As a clumping bamboo it spreads slowly outward from a tight base rather than sending out invasive runners, so no rhizome barrier is required, though large stands still eventually need room to widen. It is only moderately cold hardy for a bamboo, with foliage damage likely below roughly 15 degrees F even though the roots can survive colder snaps in zone 8. Its dense, upright-to-arching form makes it a popular privacy hedge, screen, or large container specimen in warm-climate gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting since this is a vigorous running bamboo capable of spreading well beyond its original planting site.

directions: Castillon is a striking variegated selection of giant timber bamboo, its culms colored golden-yellow with irregular green stripes concentrated along the sulcus groove, the reverse pattern from the all-yellow-culmed cultivars of the same species. Like the straight species it is a vigorous running bamboo, sending rhizomes well beyond the original clump, so a buried barrier at least 24 to 30 inches deep is essential for reliable long-term containment. It is one of the more cold-hardy giant timber bamboos, tolerating winter lows into the single digits once established, and the towering culms make it a dramatic grove or specimen planting where its color and scale can be fully appreciated. New shoots are edible when harvested young, as with the straight species.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; a deep, sturdy rhizome barrier is mandatory, as this large-diameter timber bamboo is an aggressive and fast-spreading runner even by Phyllostachys standards.

directions: Aureocaulis is a golden-culmed selection of vivax bamboo, one of the largest-diameter timber bamboos reliably grown in cold-temperate gardens, its thick yellow canes often marked with random irregular green streaks and sectors. It is among the most cold-hardy of the giant Phyllostachys, tolerating temperatures well below zero once established, which lets gardeners in cooler zones grow a true giant timber bamboo that would otherwise be limited to milder climates. It runs aggressively by underground rhizomes and requires a deep, unbroken barrier for containment; without one it can colonize surprising distances from the original planting within a few seasons. Because of its scale, it is best reserved for large properties as a grove, windbreak, or bold architectural screen rather than small residential lots.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; this short running bamboo spreads by rhizomes and benefits from a root barrier or an isolated bed to keep its low thickets in bounds.

directions: Marbled bamboo is a compact, short-statured running species named for the mottled purple-brown and cream markings on the sheaths of its young culms, an effect most visible in the first year or two of a cane's life before the sheaths fall away. Culms typically stay under six feet, giving it a fine-textured, almost fern-like presence closer to a groundcover than the towering canes typical of larger Phyllostachys relatives. Like several of its Chimonobambusa relatives, it can produce new shoots later in the growing season rather than only in spring, so patience with its seasonal habits pays off. It spreads by rhizomes and is best confined with a shallow-to-moderate root barrier, making it well suited to shaded woodland edges, Japanese-style gardens, or as a textured underplanting beneath larger bamboo groves.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this running bamboo spreads into a dense low thicket and should be contained with a rhizome barrier or a naturally bounded bed.

directions: Tessellate bamboo carries the largest leaves of any commonly cultivated cold-hardy bamboo, with individual blades reaching up to a foot or more in length, giving low plantings a bold, almost tropical texture despite the plant's serious winter hardiness. Culms stay short and slender, usually under six feet, while the broad glossy foliage does the visual work, arching outward to form a dense, weed-suppressing understory mat. It spreads by running rhizomes into a thick colony over time and should be planted with a buried barrier or confined to a bed bounded by pavement or a mowed strip. Its combination of deep shade tolerance and cold hardiness makes it valuable as a woodland floor groundcover or naturalized understory planting beneath deciduous trees where few other bamboos would survive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade with shelter from harsh wind; as a tight clumper it needs no rhizome barrier but is less cold hardy than most Phyllostachys.

directions: Kew Beauty is prized above all for the striking powdery blue-white bloom that coats its brand-new culms, a waxy coating that gradually weathers to green and then brown as the cane ages through its first year. It forms a tight, well-behaved clump in the manner of most Himalayan Thamnocalamus, with no invasive rhizome spread, making it a good choice for a specimen accent near a patio or entry where the blue new growth can be admired up close. It is noticeably less cold hardy than the large running Phyllostachys species, with foliage and culm damage possible in harder freezes, so gardeners at the cold edge of its range should site it with wind shelter and mulch the base heavily going into winter. Give it moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil and dappled protection from the harshest afternoon sun in hot climates.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; install a rhizome barrier before planting since this is a moderately vigorous running bamboo.

directions: Tootsik bamboo produces smooth, dark green culms with a distinctive zigzagging alignment of the lowest few internodes near the base, a quirk that makes older clumps easy to identify even without the foliage. It is a moderately vigorous running bamboo, less aggressive than the largest Phyllostachys timber species but still capable of spreading steadily by rhizome, so a buried barrier is recommended for anything but the most spacious plantings. It tolerates more shade than many running bamboos, thriving as an understory or courtyard planting, a trait that has made it a traditional choice around temples and shaded garden courts in Japan and China for centuries. Once established it is reliably cold hardy and makes an effective mid-height privacy screen or grove planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this is a tight clumping bamboo and needs no rhizome barrier.

directions: Chilean feather bamboo is unusual among bamboos for its solid, pith-filled culms rather than the hollow canes typical of nearly every other genus, a structural quirk that reflects its distant relation to the mainstream running and clumping bamboo groups. It forms a dense, tightly clumping vase-shaped mound with numerous slender branchlets clothed in small, fine leaves, giving the whole plant a soft, feathery texture that reads more like an ornamental grass than a typical bamboo grove. Native to the cool, wet forests of the Chilean and Argentine Andes, it tolerates cooler summers, more shade, and heavier soils than most warm-climate bamboos, and it is reliably cold hardy once established. Because it never runs, it is a good choice for gardeners who want dramatic bamboo texture as a specimen, screen, or border planting without any risk of the colony spreading beyond its footprint.
